overview.title: Chapter 15 summary: the Transformer
overview.main_topic: Final summary bullet of chapter 15: the Transformer as an attention-only sequence architecture, its stacked attention/feedforward blocks, scalability, parallel training without sequence loops, bidirectional encoders and causal decoders
overview.central_idea: The Transformer passes information across a sequence only through attention, stacks alternating attention and two-layer feedforward blocks, keeps improving with more parameters and data, trains in parallel because it has no sequence-length loop, and comes in two flavours: bidirectional encoders for representations and causal decoders for next-word prediction.
overview.importance: These five points compress sections 15.3-15.4 into a checklist and set up chapter 16, where a decoder-only Transformer (mini-GPT) is pretrained at scale. Each point explains a design choice you will reuse there.
learning_objectives: State what distinguishes the Transformer from RNNs: attention is the only cross-position mechanism
Describe the block structure: attention sublayer + two-layer feedforward network, stacked
Explain why the absence of a sequence-length loop makes training parallelizable
Distinguish bidirectional (encoder) from causal (decoder) attention and what each is used for
Connect scalability with parameters and data to the pretrained models of section 15.4 and chapter 16
prerequisites: Language modeling and RNN-based sequence models (15.1-15.2)

summary:
This page contains the **last bullet of the chapter 15 summary**; the earlier bullets (language models, masked language models, sequence-to-sequence models, attention) are on p.488.

The bullet defines the **Transformer** as a sequence modeling architecture that uses **attention as the only mechanism to pass information across a sequence**. No recurrence and no convolution move information between positions; every other operation (feedforward layers, normalization) acts on each position independently. Five sub-points follow:

1. **Structure**: the Transformer stacks blocks of **alternating attention and two-layer feedforward networks** (the encoder block of p.468 and the decoder block of p.470).
2. **Scaling**: it can grow to **many parameters and lots of training data while still improving accuracy** on language modeling, which is what made the pretrained models of section 15.4 (BERT, RoBERTa) and chapter 16 (GPT) possible.
3. **Parallelism**: unlike RNNs, it involves **no sequence-length loops at training time**, so all positions are processed at once and training is much easier to parallelize across many machines.
4. **Encoders** use **bidirectional attention** to build a rich representation of a sequence; every token can look at tokens before and after it (as in RoBERTa, p.479).
5. **Decoders** use **causal attention** to predict the next word in a language-model setup; each token can only look at earlier tokens.

The page then ends; chapter 16 (p.490) puts the decoder to work in a GPT-style text generator.

paragraphs.excerpt: The Transformer is a sequence modeling architecture that uses attention as the
paragraphs.what_it_says: The Transformer passes information across a sequence only through attention. It stacks alternating attention and two-layer feedforward blocks; it scales to many parameters and lots of data while still improving at language modeling; it has no sequence-length loops at training time, unlike RNNs, so it trains in parallel across many machines; its encoder uses bidirectional attention to build a rich representation; its decoder uses causal attention to predict the next word.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each sub-point names a property and implicitly a contrast. Attention-only communication contrasts with the RNN's hidden state carried step by step (pp.456-460). The block stack is the recipe built in 15.3.2-15.3.3. Scalability and parallelism together explain why Transformers, not RNNs, are the models trained on billions or trillions of tokens (p.484). The encoder/decoder split is a split by attention mask: no mask (bidirectional) for understanding tasks, a causal mask for generation.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: These are the design facts you need for chapter 16, where a decoder-only Transformer is pretrained on about a billion tokens (p.497). Knowing that the decoder is causal explains why it can be trained on raw text with shifted labels, and knowing there is no sequence loop explains why such training is feasible on GPUs.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: 'no sequence-length loops at training time' holds because of **teacher forcing** plus a causal mask: all $T$ next-token predictions of a sequence are computed in a single forward pass, while an RNN must compute $h_1, h_2, \dots, h_T$ one after another. At *inference* time a decoder still generates one token at a time in a loop (p.502). The cost of this parallelism is that self-attention compares every pair of positions, $O(T^2)$ in sequence length.

terminology.meaning: Every position may attend to every other position, before and after it; used in encoders such as BERT/RoBERTa.
Attention masked so position $t$ can only attend to positions $\le t$; required for next-token prediction so the model cannot see the answer.
The per-position Dense → Dense sublayer of each Transformer block, applied identically to every token.
A computation that must iterate over time steps one at a time, as an RNN does.

concepts.name: Transformer
concepts.definition: A sequence architecture in which attention is the only mechanism that moves information between positions, organized as stacked blocks of attention and per-position feedforward networks.
concepts.intuition: Instead of reading a sentence word by word and keeping a running memory, every word looks at the other words at the same time and decides which ones matter.
concepts.technical: Each block: (masked or unmasked) multi-head attention → residual + layer normalization → Dense–Dense feedforward → residual + layer normalization. Positional embeddings (p.475) supply order information, because attention by itself is order-agnostic.
concepts.significance: Scales with data and parameters and trains in parallel, which made pretrained models like BERT, RoBERTa and GPT feasible.
concepts.example: RoBERTa base (encoder, fine-tuned on p.485); the mini-GPT of chapter 16 (decoder-only).
concepts.misconception: 'No loops' applies to training; autoregressive generation still loops token by token.

concepts.name: Causal (masked) attention
concepts.definition: Attention in which each position can attend only to itself and earlier positions.
concepts.intuition: When predicting the next word you are not allowed to peek at it.
concepts.technical: Implemented by adding $-\infty$ (or a large negative number) to attention scores above the diagonal before the softmax, so their weights become 0.
concepts.significance: It lets a decoder be trained on every position of a sequence at once while still being a valid next-token predictor.
concepts.example: In 'the cat sat', the representation of 'cat' can use 'the' and 'cat' but not 'sat'.
concepts.misconception: Causal attention is not slower than bidirectional attention; it computes the same score matrix and just masks half of it.

concepts.name: Bidirectional attention
concepts.definition: Unmasked self-attention in which every position may attend to every other position.
concepts.intuition: Each word gets to read the whole sentence, before and after it, before deciding what it means.
concepts.technical: Used in Transformer encoders; combined with masked language modeling in BERT/RoBERTa pretraining (p.479).
concepts.significance: Produces rich representations for classification and tagging, but cannot be used directly for left-to-right generation.
concepts.example: RoBERTa's first-token vector summarizes the whole review because it attends to all tokens (p.485).
concepts.misconception: A bidirectional encoder is not a good next-word generator: it was never trained to predict without seeing the right context.

deeper.title: Why 'no sequence-length loop' matters so much in practice
deeper.body:
For a sequence of $T$ tokens:

- An **RNN** computes $h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t)$. Step $t$ needs the result of step $t-1$, so the $T$ steps are inherently sequential. A GPU's thousands of cores sit mostly idle, waiting for the previous step.
- A **Transformer** computes the attention scores for all pairs of positions as one matrix product $QK^\top$ of shape $T \times T$, then all outputs as another matrix product. All $T$ positions are processed together, which is exactly the kind of large dense linear algebra GPUs and TPUs are built for.

With a causal mask, a decoder trained on a sequence of 256 tokens (as in chapter 16, p.496) makes 256 next-token predictions in one forward pass. This is a big part of why Transformers could be scaled to the data sizes listed on p.484. (Explanation beyond the book.)

deeper.title: Encoder vs decoder at a glance
deeper.body:
| | Encoder | Decoder |
|---|---|---|
| Attention mask | none (bidirectional) | causal |
| Typical objective | masked language modeling (p.479) | next-token prediction (p.448) |
| Good for | representations, classification (p.485) | generation (chapter 16) |
| Book examples | RoBERTa; translation encoder (p.472) | translation decoder (p.472); mini-GPT (p.497) |

visualizations.title: Encoder and decoder blocks
visualizations.why: The summary bullet contrasts a bidirectional encoder with a causal decoder, both built from alternating attention and feedforward sublayers. Hover over the parts of the encoder-decoder Transformer to review each sublayer.

misconceptions.claim: Transformers never loop over the sequence.
misconceptions.correction: The summary says no sequence-length loops *at training time*. Generating text still loops one token at a time (p.502).

misconceptions.claim: The encoder and decoder use different kinds of attention computation.
misconceptions.correction: Both use dot-product attention; the decoder adds a causal mask (and, in sequence-to-sequence models, cross-attention to the encoder output).

misconceptions.claim: Attention-only means the Transformer has no other layers.
misconceptions.correction: Attention is the only mechanism that moves information *across positions*; each block also has a two-layer feedforward network applied to each position separately.

Transformer decoder block and causal masking.
Bidirectional encoders pretrained with masked language modeling (BERT, RoBERTa).

later.note: The GPT approach drops the encoder and keeps only the causal decoder.
Generative decoding loops one token at a time at inference.

prerequisites.note: Sequence-to-sequence learning with RNNs, the architecture the Transformer replaces.

takeaways: In a Transformer, attention is the only way information moves between positions.
The architecture is a stack of blocks alternating attention and a two-layer feedforward network.
It keeps improving as parameters and data grow, which enabled large-scale pretraining.
No sequence-length loop at training time makes it far easier to parallelize than an RNN.
Encoders use bidirectional attention for representations; decoders use causal attention for next-word prediction.

questions.question: According to the chapter summary, what is the only mechanism a Transformer uses to pass information across a sequence?
questions.explanation: The summary states attention is the only such mechanism. Recurrence belongs to RNNs, convolution is not used, and positional embeddings add order information to each token but do not move information between positions.

questions.question: Why does the absence of sequence-length loops make Transformers easier to train in parallel than RNNs?
questions.answer: An RNN must compute each hidden state from the previous one, so time steps are sequential. A Transformer processes all positions with matrix products in one pass, so the work can be spread across many cores and machines.
questions.explanation: This is the third sub-point of the summary bullet; the matrix-product detail is an explanation beyond the page.

questions.question: Which kind of attention does a Transformer decoder use to predict the next word?
questions.explanation: The decoder must not see future tokens, so its self-attention is causal. Bidirectional attention is the encoder's; cross-attention is an additional sublayer in seq2seq decoders, not the next-word mechanism by itself.

questions.question: What two sublayers alternate inside each Transformer block, according to the summary?
questions.answer: An attention layer and a two-layer feedforward network.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first sub-point; residual connections and normalization also appear in the blocks built on pp.468-471.

questions.question: Why would a bidirectional encoder like RoBERTa be a poor choice for generating text left to right?
questions.answer: It was trained with access to both left and right context; when generating, the right context does not exist yet, and nothing in its training taught it to predict the next token from the past alone.
questions.explanation: The summary pairs encoders with representations and decoders with next-word prediction; p.479 calls the encoder 'not a model meant to run generation in a loop'.

questions.question: Without looking back, can you list the five sub-points of the Transformer bullet and give one page where each was introduced?
questions.answer: Self-check: block structure (p.468), scaling (p.484 and section 15.4), no sequence loops (vs RNNs, p.456), bidirectional encoder (p.479), causal decoder (p.470).
questions.explanation: Being able to tie each claim to the chapter's code shows you have consolidated chapter 15 before starting chapter 16.
